analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to pay passengers cash compensation, rebooking, meals, and hotels for cancellations and long delays.
analysis.headline: The bill would require airlines to pay at least $750 in cash, plus free rebooking, meals, and hotel rooms, when they cancel or badly delay a flight; it has 16 cosponsors but has sat in the Senate Commerce Committee with no action since its December 2025 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill orders the Department of Transportation to write rules forcing airlines to compensate passengers when the airline itself causes a cancellation or a significant delay: at least $750 in cash, a free seat on the next available flight on any airline or other transport, meals, and — for overnight disruptions — a hotel room and rides to and from it. It directs the DOT to model the final rules on Canada's and the European Union's passenger compensation regimes, which pay $300 for delays over 3 hours and $600 for 6 or more. An interim rule would take effect two years after enactment, with a final rule to follow. The bill was introduced December 4, 2025 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has had no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers whose flights are canceled or significantly delayed for reasons attributable to the airline. Instead of a voucher (or nothing), they would be owed at least $750 in cash, free rebooking on any carrier or alternative transport, meal credits, and for overnight disruptions a hotel room and ground transportation. Travelers on foreign carriers flying to or from the U.S. are covered too. The U.S. currently has no mandated cash compensation for delays; the European Union and Canada do.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Department of Transportation to write rules obligating airlines to pay at least $750 in cash to any passenger on a flight the airline cancels or significantly delays, when the disruption is directly attributable to the airline.
Requires airlines to rebook affected passengers at no charge on any available flight — including on a competing airline — or on another means of transportation, at the earliest opportunity.
Requires airlines to cover meals, and for overnight disruptions hotel accommodations plus ground transportation to and from the hotel.

Directs the rulemaking to model compensation on Canada's Air Passenger Protection Regulations and the EU's Regulation 261/2004, which mandate minimum cash payments of $300 for delays of more than 3 hours and $600 for 6 hours or more.

Sets deadlines so the protections cannot be deferred indefinitely: a rulemaking committee within 90 days, an interim final rule within 18 months of enactment (effective two years after enactment), and semiannual progress reports to Congress until the final rule is done.

analysis.who_pays: Airlines, which would owe cash payments and covered expenses on disruptions they cause, and potentially passengers through somewhat higher fares if carriers pass the costs on. Passengers delayed by weather, air traffic control problems, or other causes outside the airline's control would not qualify for cash compensation under the bill's 'directly attributable' standard.

drawbacks.text: Compensation is owed only when a disruption is 'directly attributable' to the airline — a storm, an air traffic control problem, or another airline's failure would leave passengers with no cash compensation, and the bill leaves it to a later rulemaking to define that line.
The bill puts the airlines themselves on the Aviation Rulemaking Committee that drafts the recommendations, so carriers get a formal seat in shaping the rules that would bind them.

Relief is slow: even if enacted, the interim compensation rule would not take effect until two years after the president signs it, and the final rule would come later still, after a committee report and a separate rulemaking process.
Airlines would bear new per-disruption costs, which carriers would likely recover at least partly through higher fares — a cost spread across all travelers, including those never delayed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and well-tested: the EU and Canada have run similar mandatory compensation regimes for years without collapsing air travel, and U.S. passengers currently get only vouchers or rebooking when an airline strands them. The main design weaknesses are the narrow 'directly attributable' trigger, the airlines' formal seat at the rulemaking table, and a two-year-plus wait before any money is owed. The cost to travelers through fares is likely modest relative to the guaranteed cash recovery for those who experience a bad disruption.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, vote, or floor action; Congress is still in session, so it could still move.

narrative.text: Senator Mark Kelly introduced the bill on December 4, 2025 with 16 original cosponsors — 15 Senate Democrats and Independent Senator Bernie Sanders.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, the committee that handles airline regulation.
No further action appears in the record: no committee hearing or markup, no vote, and no Republican cosponsors as of the latest action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the airlines: no compensation rule exists, so carriers continue to owe delayed and canceled passengers only what current rules provide — rebooking and refunds, but no mandated cash compensation, meals, or hotels.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airlines, so far — no new rules yet

for.name: Mark Kelly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its compensation, rebooking, and hotel requirements.

against.name: Ted Cruz
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chairs received the bill on referral and has taken no action on it — no hearing or markup appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 sponsors are Democrats or Independents, none of the Senate's 55 Republicans has cosponsored, and the Republican-chaired Commerce Committee has not acted on the bill.

industries.note: Carriers would owe at least $750 in cash per affected passenger plus free rebooking on any airline, meals, and hotels on disruptions they cause — a new mandated liability on top of current rebooking rules. They would also get a formal seat on the rulemaking committee that drafts the recommendations, giving them influence over the rules that would bind them.
Airlines would have to provide or reimburse hotel rooms and rides for overnight disruptions, channeling new paid business to lodging and ground transport providers near airports when flights go down.

industries.industry: Foreign air carriers serving U.S. routes
industries.note: The bill expressly treats foreign carriers like U.S. airlines, so carriers flying American passengers would owe the same cash compensation and amenities for disruptions they cause.

analysis.trajectory: Most bills die in committee without a vote, and this one has shown none of the signs that break that pattern: no Republican cosponsors, no committee hearing, and no floor scheduling weeks after referral. The realistic path to a vote would run through the Commerce Committee under Republican chair Ted Cruz, which so far has not acted; absent that, the bill is likely to sit until the Congress ends, though a high-profile flight-disruption crisis could revive it.
